Startup Atoco Uses Data‑Center Waste Heat to Pull Water from Air with MOF Technology

30 Oct 2026, 05:15 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Science Desk · Source: www.wired.com

4 min read

A prototype turns low‑grade heat into drinkable water

On a sweltering September morning in Irvine, California, a 20‑foot‑tall metal‑clad unit sits in the parking lot of Atoco, a local startup. The machine, built around metal‑organic frameworks (MOFs), captures water vapor from ambient air and releases it as liquid using only modest heat – no electricity or grid connection is required for the core water‑harvesting process.

The prototype can produce up to 300 liters of water per day when supplied with heat equivalent to a 20‑kilowatt data‑center. Atoco says a commercial version could generate 1,000 liters per day, enough to offset a small portion of a data‑center’s water use.

How the technology works

MOFs are crystalline materials that act like molecular sponges. Their internal lattice – described by UC Irvine’s Seth Cohen as “a jungle gym on a playground” – contains pores that can adsorb large quantities of water molecules even when relative humidity is in the teens. Once saturated, the material feels dry to the touch and does not release water by squeezing.

To extract the captured water, Atoco applies low‑grade heat (as low as 100 °F). The heat causes the water molecules to desorb from the pores, condensing into a clear stream that the company describes as essentially distilled water. The heat source can be waste heat from industrial processes; Atoco’s demo used simulated heat at about 150 °F.

Why data‑center waste heat is a target

Modern AI‑focused data centers emit large amounts of low‑grade heat – comparable to the output of tens of thousands of homes – and consume millions of gallons of water daily for cooling. Operators typically disperse the waste heat into the environment, creating heat islands.

“Atoco’s system turns that waste heat into clean water,” says CEO Samer Taha. “We give you back water, the same product that is causing the issue.”

The company has already installed five on‑grid prototype trials with partners in the United States and the Gulf Cooperation Council. It plans to begin taking orders for its first commercial unit by the end of the year and is in talks with unnamed major tech firms that have pledged to become water‑positive by 2030.

Practical implications and comparisons

  • Energy use – Unlike silica desiccants, which require very high temperatures to release water, Atoco’s MOFs operate with modest heat, reducing the energy penalty.
  • Cost – Atoco estimates a levelized cost of $5 per metric ton of water. This is higher than the $2‑plus per ton achievable by the newest desalination plants, a gap the company expects to close in three to five years.
  • Scalability – The prototype’s 300‑liter output is modest compared to the millions of gallons per day used by large data centers. Scaling to that level would require many units operating in parallel and a reliable heat source.
  • Rural deployment – Without nearby waste heat, the system would need an external energy source to power the heating step, which could limit usefulness in off‑grid, water‑stressed communities.

Confirmed facts vs. open questions

Confirmed:

  • MOFs can adsorb water at low humidity and release it with heat as low as 100 °F.
  • Atoco’s prototype produces up to 300 L/day using heat equivalent to a 20 kW data center.
  • The company has five on‑grid trials and aims for commercial orders by year‑end.
  • Levelized water cost is quoted at $5/ton.

Uncertain / Not yet demonstrated:

  • Performance at the scale of hyperscale data centers (tens of megawatts of waste heat).
  • Long‑term durability of MOF materials under continuous cycling.
  • Exact pricing and financing terms for commercial units.
  • Real‑world water quality when operating in polluted air environments.
